segments.say: If you've ever read a magazine article about attraction, you've probably come across two exciting ideas. The first is that there's a love hormone, a chemical called oxytocin, that makes us bond and trust. The second is that we're secretly drawn to each other by invisible scents called pheromones. Both ideas have a grain of truth. And both have been wildly oversold.

show.title: Myth eight: a love hormone and secret scents

segments.say: Let's start with oxytocin, and with an unlikely hero. A small rodent called the prairie vole, found in the grasslands of North America. Unlike most rodents, prairie voles tend to form lasting pair bonds. A male and female often stay together, share a nest and raise their young together.

show.sub: A small rodent with a big reputation

segments.say: Researchers including Sue Carter, Thomas Insel and Larry Young spent years studying why. They found that two hormones, oxytocin and vasopressin, played important roles in how these voles formed bonds. Blocking their effects in the brain could stop pair bonds from forming. In 2001, Insel and Young reviewed this work in a widely read paper.

It was fascinating research, and it quickly inspired a tempting leap. If oxytocin helps voles bond, perhaps it does the same in people. Before long, newspapers were calling it the love hormone, the cuddle chemical, even the moral molecule. Researchers began giving people oxytocin as a nasal spray and measuring how they behaved.

Some of the early human studies reported eye-catching effects. People who received the spray seemed more trusting, better at reading emotions, or more generous. These findings spread rapidly through popular books and articles, and the idea of a simple love chemical took hold.
But as more researchers looked closely at the human studies, problems started to appear.

In 2016, Hasse Walum, Irwin Waldman and Larry Young himself, one of the original vole researchers, published a critical analysis of the human nasal spray studies. They argued that many of them used small samples, which makes impressive results more likely to be flukes. They concluded that many reported effects were likely to be false positives.

show.what: Statistical and methodological considerations for the interpretation of intranasal oxytocin studies

segments.say: Other reviews raised similar concerns. Some well-known findings proved hard to replicate. And there are basic open questions, such as how much oxytocin from a nasal spray actually reaches the brain. On top of that, oxytocin's effects seem to depend heavily on the person and the situation. It isn't simply a chemical that makes everyone warmer.

show.sub: Hard to replicate, unclear how it works

segments.say: In fact, some studies have suggested that oxytocin may strengthen bonds within a group while making people less warm towards outsiders. That's a long way from a universal love potion. Oxytocin is real and important. It plays roles in childbirth, breastfeeding and social behaviour. But the idea of a single love hormone is a myth.

Now to pheromones. In insects and many other animals, pheromones are well established. They're chemical signals that trigger specific responses in other members of the same species. Moths can detect them from great distances. Ants use them to mark trails.

It's natural to wonder whether humans have them too. And you may have seen perfumes advertised as containing human pheromones, promising to make you irresistible. Researchers have searched for human pheromones for decades. So, what have they found?

In 2015, the zoologist Tristram Wyatt at the University of Oxford published a review with a telling title. The search for human pheromones, the lost decades. He argued that the two chemicals most often studied as human pheromones had been chosen without solid evidence, and that the research built on them was largely unconvincing.

show.where: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2015
show.what: The search for human pheromones: the lost decades

segments.say: Two years later, Leigh Simmons and his colleagues in Australia tested those same two chemicals directly. Volunteers rated faces of the opposite sex while exposed to the supposed pheromones or to a control scent. The chemicals made no difference to how attractive people found the faces. So far, there's no solid evidence for a human sex pheromone.

show.what: Putative sex-specific human pheromones do not affect gender perception, attractiveness ratings or unfaithfulness judgements of opposite sex faces

segments.say: There's a related myth you may have heard. The idea that women who live together end up with synchronised menstrual cycles, supposedly because of chemical signals. It started with a study published in the journal Nature in 1971. But later, larger and more careful studies didn't find reliable evidence of synchrony. Apparent matches can easily happen by chance.
So does that mean smell plays no role in human connection? Not at all. It just works in less magical ways than the perfume adverts suggest.

In 1995, Claus Wedekind and his colleagues in Switzerland asked men to wear the same T-shirt for two nights. Then women smelled the T-shirts and rated how pleasant they found each scent. On average, women tended to prefer the scent of men whose immune system genes, known as the MHC, were more different from their own.

show.where: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 1995

segments.say: It's an intriguing result, and it led to the idea that smell might help steer us towards partners with complementary immune systems. But later studies have produced mixed results, and the effect, if it exists, seems small. It's best thought of as a fascinating possibility rather than a settled fact.

What's much less controversial is how powerful familiar smells can be. Many people find comfort in the scent of a partner's jumper, a parent's kitchen, or a baby's head. Smells are closely linked to memory and emotion. They might not be secret pheromones, but they can still be a quiet thread of connection.

Think of a smell that instantly takes you back to someone you love. Perhaps a particular soap, or bread baking, or rain on a garden path. That connection is real, built from memories and feelings layered over years. No perfume can bottle it, because it belongs to the two of you.

So, a love hormone and secret scents? Mostly myths. Oxytocin matters, but it's not a simple love chemical. Many of the exciting spray studies may not hold up. There's no solid evidence for a human sex pheromone, and cycle syncing hasn't been reliably supported. But smell and memory still weave quietly through our closest relationships.

show.title: What the evidence says
items: Oxytocin matters, but it is not a simple love hormone
Many nasal spray findings may be false positives
No solid evidence for a human sex pheromone
Cycle syncing is not reliably supported

segments.say: It's easy to see why these ideas are so appealing. A single chemical or scent that explained attraction would make everything simple. But human connection doesn't seem to work that way. It's built from many small things, glances, timing, shared values, familiarity, and the slow growth of trust.

And speaking of things that don't work the way we think, here's one that surprises almost everyone. Most of us feel fairly sure about what we're looking for in a partner. But when researchers compared what people said they wanted with who they were actually drawn to, the results were striking.
